title: Pieces that crossed the boards and came back
summary: Both queens on board B were lost early and crossed to board A, where Black kept its queen in hand for the rest of the game and pulled clearly ahead from 22...N@f4. After that, follow the pieces: the bishop taken on g5 on board A returns to g5 by way of d5 on board B, and the rook White on board A loses on g1 is dropped by White on board B in the mating attack that ends with P@f4#.
event: HypeBeast 1.1.1 against itself, 500,000 nodes a move for one team and 450,000 for the other

result.text: White on board B mates; the team of A-Black and B-White wins.

moves.note: Its first choice was Nxg2+. But it expected its partner on board B to win a queen, about four chances in five, and with a queen in hand it scored Ba6 well ahead of the knight check; without the queen the two moves scored about the same. The queen came one move later with Qxf3 on board B. Black never dropped it: it was still in hand when the game ended.

lines.note: White's best answer before the queen arrives: B@e2, after which the knight still takes on g2.
Its first choice: Nxg2+ Rxg2, and only then Ba6.
A search that ignores the other board plays Rf8, which scored worse than Ba6 when both were searched the same way.
With the queen in hand: the bishops come off on f1 and the engine scored the position slightly in Black's favour.

moves.note: White takes the queen on f3, which had just captured the bishop dropped there with B@f3. The queen goes to Black on board A, as Black there had counted on when it played Ba6, and Black keeps it in hand for the rest of the game.

Its first choice was Qxf7+. It gave the queen for the knight on d7 instead, because in the case where a pawn reached it from board A it scored this capture far higher. A pawn came at once from Bxe3, and White dropped a pawn on g2 on its next move. The queen went to White on board A, who dropped it with Q@g4.

On board B its partner had just given up the queen with Qxd7+, so after the forced Kxd7 White here would have a queen to drop; the engine thought that very likely. With a white queen coming, it scored its first choice g6 much worse than Bxe3, which takes the pawn on e3 and sends it to its partner. The queen did arrive, and White dropped it on move 23 with Q@g4.

lines.note: White's best answer by the reply search: N@g4, and the bishop takes the rook on g1.
Its first choice, g6, scored about level before the arriving queen was counted.
The plan with a white queen assumed in hand: after B@f2, Black drops its own queen on f4 and White answers Q@g3.

moves.note: Its first choice was P@e3+. Expecting a knight to reach it from board B, it dropped the knight it held on f4 first and played P@e3+ on its next move. No knight came. From this move on, Black's own score on board A never fell below about six pawns in its favour.

This is the queen that crossed from board B and was dropped with Q@g4. It takes the bishop that had just captured with Bxg5, and that bishop goes to Black on board B, who drops it with B@d5. White had little choice: the other two moves it compared, a3 and Qxf4+, were mated in its search. It gave about even chances that a knight would reach Black here, and one came at once from hxg5 on board B. After P@f6 and Qh4, Black dropped it with N@g6 and White's score fell sharply.

lines.note: What it expected at the time, with no knight in Black's hand: P@f6 Qh4 Ng6.
Black's plan at its next turn, with the knight from board B in hand: N@g6, which the engine scored about eleven pawns in Black's favour.

moves.note: The first move of its search was Bxe4, taking the knight on e4; given more time on the same decision it switched to Ne5. White answered Nxd5, taking the bishop that had come from board A, and by Black's next turn its score had dropped sharply. Its search had scored Bxe4 and Ne5 about the same, so the lines show the refutation but no clear way out. The bishop went to Black on board A, who dropped it back on g5.

lines.note: White's answer by the reply search: P@f5, with Nxd5 a move later.
Its search's first choice, Bxe4, before the longer look changed it.
A search that ignores the other board plays Be5, which scored a little worse than Ne5 searched the same way.
White's plan at its next turn: Nxd5, and after cxd5 the pawn check g6+.

moves.note: Its first choice was Q@g5, the queen that came over with Qxf3 on board B. It dropped the bishop on the same square instead, scoring it a little better if a knight reached White. This is the bishop Qxg5 captured on g5: Black on board B dropped it with B@d5, White took it there with Nxd5, and now it is back.

On its own board the engine scored Black roughly level, but its partner on board A was about twenty pawns down by a quick count, and the engine counted any piece Black lost here as enough for its opponents to mate there. Almost all of its large minus score came from that. P@e7 hits the knight on d6, and that pawn later took it with exd6. The search that ignores the other board chose Nd5 and scored a little worse.

lines.note: Its own main line: White takes on c6, the pawn takes the knight on d6, and a run of exchanges follows.
A search that ignores the other board plays Nd5, which scored slightly worse than P@e7 searched the same way.
If a queen had reached White here it would play b5, and White drops the queen on g3; no queen came.

moves.note: On board A, by the engine's quick count, one more piece of any kind would let its partner mate, so it valued every capture here as a gift to its partner, and most of its score for Bxc6 came from that. The pawn reached Black on board A at once, but no mate came there. A search that ignores the other board preferred Bb3+, and searched the same way it scored far better than Bxc6. White still won board B.

lines.note: Its main line: exd6 Nxd6, then the bishop takes the rook on a8.
A search that ignores the other board plays Bb3+, and searched the same way it scored far better than Bxc6.

moves.note: Lost on board A by its own count, White checks with the pawn its partner had just won on board B with Nxf7. The search that ignores the other board threw in B@e8+ and N@d8+, pieces Black would take and pass to its partner, and it scored worse when searched the same way. Black took with Nxe6, so the pawn went straight back to White on board B, who dropped a pawn on f7 with check again two moves later.

lines.note: Its main line: Nxe6, and Black soon promotes on g1 with check.
A search that ignores the other board gives up a bishop, a knight and the queen to checks that are all taken.

moves.note: The knight came from board B, where White sacrificed it with Nh6+ and its partner took it with gxh6. Still lost by its own count, White dropped it on f4. Black took it two moves later with Bxf4, and it went straight back to White on board B, the side that had given it up. The search that ignores the other board chose B@d2, which scored about a pawn better searched the same way, a small gap in a lost position.

lines.note: What it expected: Black promotes on g1 taking the rook, then drops a knight on h2 and a queen on f2.
A search that ignores the other board plays B@d2, about a pawn better by the same kind of search.

moves.note: Black promotes while taking the rook on g1. The rook goes to White on board B, who drops it two moves later with R@f6+ in the mating attack.

White had three knights in hand, one of them sent over by Bxf4 on board A. N@e4+ starts a mate in three by the engine's count; the other move it compared, N@d3, did not mate. The game reached the mate by a different route, with pawn drops on e3 and f4.

lines.note: Its mating line, with knight checks instead of the pawn drops the game used.

moves.note: Board B was lost for its partner and White was far behind here. Its first choice was B@d2, but then Black could play fxg1=Q, taking the queen on g1, and that queen would go to White on board B for Q@g3+ and mate. So it checked with B@f7+ instead. Black answered by sitting in check for a moment, as bughouse allows, and then took the bishop.

lines.note: The reply search: Black takes the bishop and keeps attacking with a queen drop on e3.
Its first choice, B@d2, with its main line.
A search that ignores the other board plays B@c1 and allows fxg1=Q, the capture that would have fed the mate on board B.

moves.note: The pawn check drives the king to e5, and P@f4# follows. The search that ignores the other board found Nxh6+, also a mate in two.

lines.note: The game's finish: Ke5 and the second pawn drop.
The other mate in two, found by a search that ignores the other board.

moves.note: In check from the bishop, Black sat for about a second. Its partner had a mate in one on board B, and while Black sat, White here could not move, so nothing could be captured and sent to the king being mated. Its clock was a little ahead of Black's clock on board B, enough to afford the wait. When its partner was on turn to mate, it took the bishop, which went to board B too.
Mate with a pawn. The bishop that had just arrived from Kxf7 on board A was not needed: the pawns were already in White's hand.
